briefs.description: R3: the rainscreen brief (depth and stagger inputs, thermal-break rule, minimise solar gain); decomposition and the input sliders.
briefs.userPrompt: Set up the inputs for a staggered rainscreen facade. Inputs: panel course depth 0.1 to 0.4 m and horizontal stagger 0 to 0.5 of a panel width (both mine). Rule: the thermal break behind the panels must stay continuous. Principle: alternate course depths to break up the facade. Evaluation: minimise solar gain on the south facade, which I will check with an annual radiation study. Start by adding the depth and stagger sliders.

briefs.description: Attractor grid: grid of points, circles whose radius shrinks with distance to an attractor; needs discovery of several components.
briefs.userPrompt: Build an attractor grid: a rectangular grid of points (5 to 20 points per side, spacing 1 to 3 m) and a circle at every point whose radius shrinks with the distance to an attractor point. Inputs: grid count, spacing, attractor x and y. Rule: radius = distance remapped into 0.1 to 0.5 m. Principle: an attractor-driven perforation pattern. Evaluation: keep every radius at least 0.1 m. Build it.

briefs.description: R5: the user locked the radius slider; a request to change it must leave the canvas unchanged and say it is locked.
A plugin that is not installed (Weaverbird): the model checks the loaded libraries and says so instead of inventing components.

briefs.userPrompt: Make a 2D Voronoi paving pattern: 30 random points inside a 20 x 20 m rectangle, with the Voronoi cells clipped to it. Inputs: point count 10 to 50 and a random seed (mine). Rule: cells stay inside the rectangle. Principle: a random cellular partition for paving. Evaluation: keep the cell count equal to the point count. Build it.

What does the Graph Mapper component do, and when would I use it?

Graph Mapper (Params > Input) remaps a list of numbers through an editable curve. You feed values in a known domain (usually 0–1) into the input, pick a graph type (Linear, Bezier, Sine, Gaussian, Parabola, Perlin, Conic, Sinc…), drag the control handles, and the output is each value re-evaluated through that curve, mapped from the input domain to the output domain you set in its context menu.

Use it when you want to shape a distribution without writing a formula:
- Attractor-style falloff: Range → Graph Mapper → panel/opening sizes, so density eases in rather than varying linearly.
- Easing along a curve: parameters from Divide Curve go through a Bezier to bunch elements near one end.
- Profiles for lofts or sections: a Gaussian or Sine graph driving scale factors gives a swelling/tapering form.
- Quick noise: Perlin for organic jitter in heights or rotations.

What does the Graph Mapper component do, and when would I use it?

Graph Mapper remaps a list of numbers through a curve you draw. Feed it values in a source domain (default 0–1), and each value is pushed through the graph (Linear, Bezier, Sine, Gaussian, Parabola, Perlin, etc.) to a target domain. You drag the handles on the component to reshape the curve interactively, so it's a way to sculpt a distribution by eye instead of writing an expression.

Typical uses:
- Attractor-free falloffs: turn a uniform Series or Range (e.g. 0–1 along a facade) into an ease-in/ease-out of panel rotations, openings, or heights.
- Non-linear spacing: remap Divide Curve parameters so contour lines bunch toward one end.
- Rescaling raw analysis data: push a distance or radiation list through a Gaussian or Sine graph before it drives geometry.
- Quick "tuning" of any 0–1 factor where the exact function doesn't matter but the feel does.

What does the Graph Mapper component do, and when would I use it?

Graph Mapper remaps a list of numbers through a curve you draw. Input values in its domain (default 0–1) are read along the X axis, the output is the curve's Y at that point. Double-click it to pick a curve type (Linear, Bezier, Sine, Gaussian, Parabola, Perlin, Conic, etc.) and drag the handles; right-click to set input/output domains.

Use it when you want a non-linear distribution without writing an expression:
- Easing a Range or Series (0–1 from Range → Graph Mapper → Bezier) so panel sizes, offsets, or rotations ramp smoothly instead of linearly.
- Attractor-style falloff: normalized distance in → Gaussian or Sine out → scale factor.
- Shaping a profile: parameter along a curve → Graph Mapper → height/width of sections.
- Any place where you'd otherwise tweak a formula by trial; the curve is a visual knob.
